recipes.title: Nigerian Party Jollof Rice
recipes.subtitle: Smoky, deep-red, every grain separate, the way it tastes at a Lagos party.
recipes.story: Party jollof is the dish every Nigerian celebration is judged by. What makes it “party” is patience: a pepper base fried until the oil rises, rice steamed rather than boiled, and a little smoky “bottom pot” at the end. We will walk you through every one of those moments.
allergens: Milk (optional butter)
Check stock cubes: some contain wheat, soy or celery
dietary: Gluten-free if your stock cubes are

hero.brief: Finished party jollof in a wide Mcuire pot, steam rising, sliced tomato and onion rings on top. Overhead, natural light.

gallery.alt: Plated: jollof, peppered chicken thigh, fried plantain, side salad. 45° angle on a Mcuire plate.
gallery.brief: Plated: jollof, peppered chicken thigh, fried plantain, side salad. 45° angle on a Mcuire plate.

gallery.alt: Close-up of grains: separate, glossy, orange-red, a few darker smoky grains.
gallery.brief: Close-up of grains: separate, glossy, orange-red, a few darker smoky grains.

equipment.name: Large heavy-bottomed pot with a lid
equipment.note: At least 5 litres for 6 servings. A thin pot burns the bottom before the top is cooked.

equipment.name: Blender
equipment.note: Any kitchen blender. A stick blender works too.

equipment.name: Aluminium foil
equipment.note: Goes under the lid to trap steam. Parchment paper also works.

equipment.name: Wooden spoon or flat spatula
equipment.note: A flat edge helps you scrape and fold.

equipment.name: Measuring cups and spoons
equipment.note: Helpful the first time. Later you will cook by eye.

ingredients.name: Ripe plum tomatoes
ingredients.note: Soft, deep red tomatoes give the best colour.

substitutes.name: 1 × 400 g tin of plum tomatoes
substitutes.note: Drain off half the juice. Works year-round.

ingredients.name: Red bell peppers (tatashe)
ingredients.note: Tatashe gives jollof its deep red colour without extra heat.

substitutes.name: Roasted red peppers from a jar
substitutes.note: Use about 300 g, drained.

ingredients.name: Scotch bonnet peppers (ata rodo)
ingredients.note: One gives a gentle warmth. Two is properly Nigerian. Remove the seeds for less heat.

substitutes.name: Habanero pepper
substitutes.note: Very similar heat and fruity flavour.

substitutes.name: ½ tsp dried chilli flakes
substitutes.note: For a milder pot. Add with the spices instead of blending.

substitutes.name: Any brown or white onion
substitutes.note: Works exactly the same.

ingredients.name: Vegetable oil
ingredients.note: Jollof needs this much oil to fry the base properly. Don’t cut it in half.

substitutes.name: Sunflower, canola or groundnut oil
substitutes.note: Any neutral oil.

ingredients.name: Tomato paste
ingredients.note: The concentrated kind in a tin or tube, not passata.

ingredients.name: Long-grain parboiled rice
ingredients.note: Also sold as “converted” or “easy-cook” rice. It stays separate and doesn’t go mushy, which is why Nigerian cooks use it.

substitutes.name: Basmati rice
substitutes.note: Use about ¼ less stock and check it 5 minutes earlier. It cooks faster and softer.

substitutes.name: Long-grain white rice
substitutes.note: Rinse very well and use ¼ less stock.

ingredients.name: Chicken stock, warm
ingredients.note: Homemade stock from boiling your chicken is best.

substitutes.name: Water + 1 extra stock cube
substitutes.note: Completely fine for a first attempt.

substitutes.name: Vegetable stock
substitutes.note: For a vegetarian pot.

ingredients.name: Chicken stock cubes
ingredients.note: Nigerian cooks often use Knorr or Maggi cubes. Check the label for allergens.

substitutes.name: 2 tsp chicken bouillon powder
substitutes.note: Same job, measure instead of crumble.

ingredients.name: Nigerian-style curry powder
ingredients.note: Milder and more yellow than Indian curry powder. It adds aroma, not heat.

substitutes.name: 1 tsp mild Madras curry powder + a pinch of turmeric
substitutes.note: Closest supermarket match.

substitutes.name: Leave them out
substitutes.note: You’ll lose a little fragrance but the jollof still works.

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.note: Add a little, taste, then add more. Stock cubes are already salty.

substitutes.name: Black pepper
substitutes.note: Use a little less.

ingredients.name: Butter
ingredients.note: Gives a glossy, rich finish.

substitutes.name: Skip it
substitutes.note: Dairy-free and still delicious.

steps.title: Set everything out before you start
steps.body: Wash your hands. Then take out every ingredient and every piece of equipment on the list and put them where you can reach them. Open the tomato paste. Unwrap the stock cubes. Measure the oil, stock and spices into cups or small bowls.
steps.why: Once the frying starts, jollof moves quickly. If you are searching for the curry powder while the tomato paste is frying, it can burn.

media.alt: Every jollof ingredient laid out on the Mcuire counter, labelled, in small bowls. Overhead.
media.brief: Every jollof ingredient laid out on the Mcuire counter, labelled, in small bowls. Overhead.

tips.text: In our kitchen we call this “setting your station”. Every Mcuire chef does it before every service, even for a dish they have cooked a thousand times.

cues.see: Every ingredient measured into its own cup or bowl, the tomato paste open and the stock cubes unwrapped, all within arm’s reach of the stove.

steps.title: Blend the pepper base
steps.body: Roughly cut the tomatoes, red peppers and the red onion into big chunks. Pull the stalk off the scotch bonnet. Put everything into the blender with 2–3 tablespoons of water (just enough to get it moving). Blend until completely smooth.

cues.see: A smooth, bright orange-red liquid with no visible chunks or pepper skins.
cues.texture: Like a thin smoothie.

media.alt: 10-second clip: blender running, then pouring the smooth pepper base so the texture is visible.
media.brief: 10-second clip: blender running, then pouring the smooth pepper base so the texture is visible.

tips.text: Scotch bonnet is very hot. After cutting it, wash your hands with soap before you touch your face or eyes.
For a milder jollof, cut the scotch bonnet open and scrape out the seeds and white inside before blending. That’s where most of the heat is.

checkpoint.question: Does your blend look like this?

options.label: Chunky, I can see bits

media.alt: Blender jug showing a chunky, uneven blend with visible pepper pieces.
media.brief: Blender jug showing a chunky, uneven blend with visible pepper pieces.

options.guidance: Blend for another 30–60 seconds. If the blades are spinning but nothing moves, add one more tablespoon of water.

options.label: Smooth and even

media.alt: Spoon lifted from a perfectly smooth pepper base.
media.brief: Spoon lifted from a perfectly smooth pepper base.

options.guidance: Perfect. Move on.

options.label: Very thin and watery

media.alt: Pepper base so thin it looks like juice.
media.brief: Pepper base so thin it looks like juice.

options.guidance: No problem. You added a bit too much water. You’ll just boil it a few minutes longer in the next step.

steps.title: Boil the pepper base down until thick
steps.body: Pour the blended pepper base into your big pot. Turn the heat to medium-high and let it bubble with the lid OFF. Stir every 3–4 minutes, scraping the bottom. You are boiling away water so the mixture becomes thick.

cues.see: The level in the pot drops by about half. It turns from bright orange to a deeper red.
cues.hear: Thick “plop-plop” bubbles instead of a rolling boil.
cues.texture: Like a loose porridge. A spoon dragged across the bottom leaves a trail for a second.

media.alt: Pepper base at the start: thin and bright, pot nearly full.
media.brief: Pepper base at the start: thin and bright, pot nearly full.

media.alt: Pepper base reduced by half: thick, deeper red, spoon trail visible.
media.brief: Pepper base reduced by half: thick, deeper red, spoon trail visible.

tips.text: It will splutter. Tilt the lid over the pot, leaving a gap, so steam can escape but the splashes stay in.
Use this time to do the next step: washing the rice.
You can make the pepper base a day ahead and keep it in the fridge. It even freezes for a month.

options.label: Still watery

media.alt: Pepper base still thin and splashy, level barely dropped.
media.brief: Pepper base still thin and splashy, level barely dropped.

options.guidance: Keep boiling with the lid off. Check again in 5 minutes. Watery base is the #1 reason jollof turns out soggy.

options.label: Thicker, but still runs fast

media.alt: Pepper base partly reduced, still runs off the spoon quickly.
media.brief: Pepper base partly reduced, still runs off the spoon quickly.

options.guidance: Almost there. Give it 3–5 more minutes.

options.label: Thick, spoon leaves a trail

media.alt: Pepper base correctly reduced, spoon trail across pot base.
media.brief: Pepper base correctly reduced, spoon trail across pot base.

options.guidance: That’s it. Turn off the heat and pour it into a bowl. You’ll need the pot for the next stage.

options.label: Sticking or catching

media.alt: Pepper base too dry, dark patches catching on the pot bottom.
media.brief: Pepper base too dry, dark patches catching on the pot bottom.

options.guidance: Turn the heat down and stir in ¼ cup of water straight away. Don’t scrape any black bits from the bottom into the sauce.

troubleshooting.fix: Turn the heat down to medium and half-cover with the lid.
Pour it into a clean pot without scraping the bottom, add a splash of water and continue on lower heat.

steps.title: Wash the rice until the water is clearer
steps.body: Put the rice in a large bowl and cover with cold water. Rub the rice between your hands for about 10 seconds. The water will turn cloudy. Tip the cloudy water out, keeping the rice in the bowl with your hand. Do this 3–4 times. Then pour the rice into a sieve and leave it to drain.
steps.why: The cloudiness is loose starch. Washing it off is what keeps your jollof grains separate instead of sticky.

cues.see: The water goes from milky-white to almost clear.

media.alt: Side by side: first wash (milky water) vs fourth wash (nearly clear water) in a glass bowl.
media.brief: Side by side: first wash (milky water) vs fourth wash (nearly clear water) in a glass bowl.

tips.text: It doesn’t have to be perfectly clear. “Clearer” is enough.

checkpoint.question: How does your water look now?

options.label: Still milky white

media.alt: Bowl of rice with milky water.
media.brief: Bowl of rice with milky water.

options.guidance: Wash it 1–2 more times.

options.label: Mostly clear

media.alt: Bowl of rice with nearly clear water.
media.brief: Bowl of rice with nearly clear water.

options.guidance: Great. Drain it in the sieve and leave it there.

steps.title: Soften the onion in hot oil
steps.body: Put the empty pot back on medium heat and pour in the oil. Wait 1–2 minutes for the oil to heat up. Test it by dropping in one slice of onion. If it sizzles gently, it’s ready. Add all the sliced onion and stir. Cook, stirring now and then, until the onion is soft.

cues.see: Onion turns soft and see-through, with the edges just starting to turn golden.
cues.hear: A steady, gentle sizzle, not loud crackling.

media.alt: Sliced onion in oil, soft and translucent with golden edges.
media.brief: Sliced onion in oil, soft and translucent with golden edges.

tips.text: If the onion goes brown in under a minute, your heat is too high. Turn it down a little before the next step.

steps.title: Fry the tomato paste until it darkens
steps.body: Add the tomato paste to the onions and stir it into the oil. Keep stirring, almost constantly, scraping the bottom of the pot. The paste will slowly change colour. Don’t rush this part. Frying the paste is what removes the sour “raw tomato” taste.

cues.see: Bright tomato red slowly becomes a deeper brick red. It may start to stick to the bottom slightly.
cues.smell: Sharp and sour at first, then sweeter and richer.

media.alt: 15-second clip: stirring tomato paste in oil; colour change from bright red to brick red.
media.brief: 15-second clip: stirring tomato paste in oil; colour change from bright red to brick red.

tips.text: It’s ready when it is a darker brick red, smells sweet rather than sharp, and the oil around the edges looks red.

checkpoint.question: What colour is your paste now?

options.label: Still bright red

media.alt: Tomato paste just added: bright, shiny, tomato red.
media.brief: Tomato paste just added: bright, shiny, tomato red.

options.guidance: Keep stirring for another 2–3 minutes.

options.label: Deeper, brick red

media.alt: Tomato paste correctly fried: deep brick red, oil tinted red at edges.
media.brief: Tomato paste correctly fried: deep brick red, oil tinted red at edges.

options.guidance: Perfect. Go straight to the next step.

options.label: Dark brown with black bits

media.alt: Overfried tomato paste: dark brown, black specks.
media.brief: Overfried tomato paste: dark brown, black specks.

options.guidance: Turn off the heat. If it smells bitter, wipe the pot and start this step again. A bitter base ruins the whole pot. A few dark specks with no bitter smell are fine. Add the pepper base now.

steps.title: Fry the pepper base until the oil rises
steps.body: Stand back a little and pour the thick pepper base into the pot. It will splutter. Stir well. Add the bay leaves, thyme and curry powder. Leave the lid off and let it cook on medium heat, stirring every 2–3 minutes and scraping the bottom each time.
steps.why: This is the most important step in the whole recipe. Rushing it is why jollof tastes raw or sour. Wait for the oil.

cues.see: A layer of red oil appears on top and around the edges of the pot. The sauce looks darker and glossy.
cues.smell: Rich and savoury, not like fresh tomatoes any more.
cues.texture: Thick enough that it holds its shape for a moment when you stir.

media.alt: Close-up: red oil separated and floating on top of fried pepper base, pooled at the pot edge.
media.brief: Close-up: red oil separated and floating on top of fried pepper base, pooled at the pot edge.

media.alt: 10-second clip: pushing the sauce aside with a spoon to show oil pooling.
media.brief: 10-second clip: pushing the sauce aside with a spoon to show oil pooling.

tips.text: At Mcuire we say: “the oil will tell you when it’s ready.” Until you see red oil on top, keep frying.
If it starts to stick and darken quickly, lower the heat. Don’t add water yet.

checkpoint.question: Can you see oil floating on top?

options.label: No oil, sauce looks wet

media.alt: Pepper sauce just added: wet, no visible oil.
media.brief: Pepper sauce just added: wet, no visible oil.

options.guidance: Keep frying and stirring every few minutes. This can take 15 minutes. That’s normal.

options.label: A little oil at the edges

media.alt: Pepper sauce with thin oil beginning at the pot edge.
media.brief: Pepper sauce with thin oil beginning at the pot edge.

options.guidance: Nearly there. 3–5 more minutes.

options.label: Red oil clearly on top

media.alt: Fried pepper sauce with clear layer of red oil on top.
media.brief: Fried pepper sauce with clear layer of red oil on top.

options.guidance: Beautiful. This is the moment. Move on.

troubleshooting.problem: It’s been 20 minutes and still no oil
troubleshooting.fix: Your base was probably still watery. Keep going, it will come. Or, if your sauce is very thick already, it may just need 2 tablespoons more oil.

steps.title: Season the sauce and taste
steps.body: Crumble in the stock cubes. Add the salt and white pepper. Pour in the warm stock and stir. Turn the heat up and let it come to a boil. Now taste it with a clean spoon (careful, it’s hot).
steps.why: The sauce should taste a little too salty and too strong on its own. The rice will soak up the flavour. If the sauce tastes “just right” now, the rice will taste bland.

cues.see: A loose, red, bubbling sauce.
cues.smell: Savoury and warm, with curry and thyme.

media.alt: Seasoned jollof sauce at a rolling boil before rice goes in.
media.brief: Seasoned jollof sauce at a rolling boil before rice goes in.

tips.text: It’s ready when it’s boiling and tastes slightly stronger and saltier than you’d want to eat by itself.

troubleshooting.problem: It tastes too salty, not just slightly
troubleshooting.fix: Add ½ cup of water and taste again. Remember the rice will absorb some salt.
Add half a stock cube or a pinch of salt and taste again.

steps.title: Add the rice and check the liquid level
steps.body: Tip in the drained rice and stir well so every grain is coated in red sauce. Then use your spoon to press the rice down flat. Now look closely. The liquid should come just to the top of the rice, not cover it like soup.

cues.see: The rice surface is flat. Liquid is just visible between the top grains, but the rice is not floating.

media.alt: Rice pressed flat in sauce with liquid exactly level with the top of the rice.
media.brief: Rice pressed flat in sauce with liquid exactly level with the top of the rice.

tips.text: Simple test: touch the surface lightly with the tip of a clean spoon. If liquid rises above the rice by more than a few millimetres, there’s too much.
Too little water is easy to fix later. Too much water makes soggy jollof. When in doubt, use less.

options.label: Rice is under liquid

media.alt: Too much liquid: rice submerged like soup.
media.brief: Too much liquid: rice submerged like soup.

options.guidance: Spoon some liquid out into a cup until it’s level with the rice. Keep it nearby in case you need it later.

options.label: Liquid just at the rice

media.alt: Correct: liquid level with the rice surface.
media.brief: Correct: liquid level with the rice surface.

options.guidance: Exactly right. Next step.

options.label: Rice looks dry on top

media.alt: Too little liquid: dry grains on top, sauce only at the bottom.
media.brief: Too little liquid: dry grains on top, sauce only at the bottom.

options.guidance: Add ¼ cup of water or stock, stir once, and press flat again.

steps.title: Cover tightly and steam on low
steps.body: Lay a sheet of foil over the top of the pot and press it down around the edges. Put the lid on top of the foil. Turn the heat down to LOW. Now leave it alone. Don’t open it and don’t stir it.
steps.why: Party jollof is steamed, not boiled. The foil traps steam so the grains cook evenly. Stirring now breaks the grains and makes it mushy.

cues.hear: Very quiet bubbling. If you hear loud boiling, the heat is too high.
cues.smell: After about 15 minutes it smells toasty and savoury.

media.alt: Pot covered with foil pressed around the rim, lid on top, low flame.
media.brief: Pot covered with foil pressed around the rim, lid on top, low flame.

tips.text: If you smell burning before the timer ends, your heat is too high. Turn it to the lowest setting. Don’t open the pot.
Good time to fry your plantain or warm your chicken.

steps.title: Check the rice and turn it gently
steps.body: Take off the lid and foil. Taste a few grains from the top. Then slide your spatula down to the bottom of the pot and gently lift and fold the rice over, from bottom to top, in 4–5 places. Don’t stir in circles. Cover again with the foil and lid and cook on low for 10 more minutes.

cues.see: Grains are swollen, orange-red, and mostly separate.
cues.texture: Soft on the outside with a very slight firmness in the middle.

media.alt: 15-second clip: folding jollof from the bottom with a flat spatula, showing correct gentle motion.
media.brief: 15-second clip: folding jollof from the bottom with a flat spatula, showing correct gentle motion.

checkpoint.question: How does the rice feel when you bite it?

options.label: Hard and the pot looks dry

media.alt: Undercooked jollof: hard white centres, dry surface.
media.brief: Undercooked jollof: hard white centres, dry surface.

options.guidance: Sprinkle ¼ cup of water over the top (don’t pour it in one spot). Cover and give it the full 10 minutes, then check again.

options.label: Soft outside, firm middle

media.alt: Nearly done jollof: grains swollen, slight bite.
media.brief: Nearly done jollof: grains swollen, slight bite.

options.guidance: Exactly where it should be. The last 10 minutes will finish it.

options.label: Soft and wet or mushy

media.alt: Overly wet jollof: grains soft and clumping.
media.brief: Overly wet jollof: grains soft and clumping.

options.guidance: Don’t add anything and don’t stir. Leave the lid off, keep the heat low, and let the extra water steam away for 5–8 minutes.

steps.title: Make the smoky “party” finish
steps.body: Optional, but this is what makes it taste like party jollof. Add the butter on top. Lay the sliced tomatoes and onion rings over the rice. Cover again. Turn the heat up to medium for 3–5 minutes without stirring. The rice touching the bottom will toast and give a gentle smoky smell.

cues.smell: Toasty and slightly smoky, like bread toasted just past golden.
cues.hear: A light crackle from the bottom of the pot.

media.alt: Sliced tomato and onion rings laid over jollof with butter melting.
media.brief: Sliced tomato and onion rings laid over jollof with butter melting.

tips.text: At Nigerian parties, jollof is cooked in huge pots over firewood. That smoky “bottom pot” flavour is what everyone is chasing. This step is how you get it at home.
If the smell turns sharp or bitter, switch off the heat immediately. When you serve, don’t scrape up the very bottom layer.

steps.title: Rest it, then fluff
steps.body: Turn off the heat. Leave the pot covered for 5–10 minutes. Then remove the bay leaves and gently fluff the rice with a fork or spatula, lifting from the bottom.
steps.why: Resting lets the last of the steam settle into the grains so they firm up and separate.

media.alt: Jollof rice, cooked
media.brief: Fluffing finished jollof with a fork: separate, glossy grains.

cues.see: Separate, glossy orange-red grains that tumble off the spatula, with a few darker, smoky grains from the bottom of the pot.
cues.smell: Sweet, smoky and peppery, with bay leaf and thyme.
cues.texture: Soft with a very slight bite. No hard centres and no mush.

steps.title: Serve it like Mcuire
steps.body: Spoon the jollof onto plates. Serve with chicken, fried plantain and a simple salad or coleslaw. You can share some of the smoky bottom-pot rice too, as long as it isn’t burnt black.

cues.see: Deep orange-red grains, separate and glossy, not wet. A few darker smoky grains are a good sign.

media.brief: Mcuire plating: jollof, peppered chicken, dodo, salad on a Mcuire plate. 45°.

tips.text: Leftovers keep 3 days in the fridge. Reheat with a splash of water, covered, until steaming hot all the way through.

options.label: Red, separate, glossy grains

media.alt: Perfect finished jollof close-up.
media.brief: Perfect finished jollof close-up.

options.guidance: You did it. That is party jollof.

options.label: Paler / more orange than red

media.alt: Pale orange jollof for comparison.
media.brief: Pale orange jollof for comparison.

options.guidance: Still delicious! Next time, use one more red pepper and fry the tomato paste a minute or two longer for a deeper colour.

options.label: A bit soft or sticky

media.alt: Soft, slightly sticky jollof for comparison.
media.brief: Soft, slightly sticky jollof for comparison.

options.guidance: Next time, start with a little less stock in step 9 and wash the rice one more time. Your flavour is the hard part, and you have it.

recipes.title: Nigerian Fried Rice
recipes.subtitle: Golden curry rice tossed with bright vegetables, prawns and liver, the party classic.
recipes.story: Next to jollof at every Nigerian party is a tray of golden fried rice. Two things make it work: rice cooked in stock until just tender, then cooled so the grains stay separate, and vegetables cut small and fried quickly so they stay crunchy and bright.
allergens: Shellfish (prawns, optional)
Milk (butter)
Check stock cubes: some contain wheat, soy or celery
dietary: Gluten-free if your stock cubes are
Leave out prawns and liver for vegetarian (use vegetable stock)

hero.brief: Golden fried rice with green, orange and yellow vegetables, prawns on top, in a serving dish. Overhead.

gallery.alt: Fried rice and jollof side by side on a party plate with chicken and dodo.
gallery.brief: Fried rice and jollof side by side on a party plate with chicken and dodo.

equipment.name: Very large frying pan or wok
equipment.note: Bigger is better. Rice needs room to fry, not steam.

substitutes.name: Basmati rice
substitutes.note: Use ¼ less stock and cook 5 minutes less.

ingredients.name: Nigerian-style curry powder
ingredients.note: This is what makes it golden.

substitutes.name: Mild curry powder + ½ tsp turmeric
Bouillon powder
substitutes.note: 1 tsp per cube.

substitutes.name: Diced cooked chicken
substitutes.note: Add with the spring onions just to warm through.

ingredients.name: Chicken or beef liver, diced
ingredients.note: Traditional in Nigerian fried rice, but optional.

steps.title: Wash the rice and chop the vegetables
steps.body: Wash the rice in a bowl of cold water 3–4 times until the water is mostly clear, then drain. Dice the carrots, green beans, green pepper and onion into small pieces, about the size of a pea, so everything is roughly the same size as the peas and corn.
steps.why: Small, even pieces cook quickly and evenly, and look beautiful mixed through the rice.

media.alt: Diced vegetables in separate small bowls, all pea-sized.
media.brief: Diced vegetables in separate small bowls, all pea-sized.

media.alt: 10-second clip: dicing a carrot into pea-sized pieces.
media.brief: 10-second clip: dicing a carrot into pea-sized pieces.

cues.see: The rinse water goes from cloudy to nearly clear. The vegetables are all diced to the size of a pea, so the board looks like confetti.

steps.title: Cook the rice in curry stock
steps.body: Put the rice in the pot with the stock, curry powder, thyme and 1 crumbled stock cube. Stir once, bring to a boil, then cover and turn the heat to low. Cook until the liquid is absorbed and the rice is just tender, with a tiny bit of bite.

cues.see: Bright golden-yellow rice, liquid gone.
cues.texture: Tender but still firm. Not soft or mushy.

media.alt: Golden curry rice in the pot, liquid just absorbed.
media.brief: Golden curry rice in the pot, liquid just absorbed.

checkpoint.question: Taste a few grains. How are they?

options.label: Crunchy in the middle

media.alt: Undercooked rice with chalky centres.
media.brief: Undercooked rice with chalky centres.

options.guidance: Add 3 tablespoons of water, cover and cook 3–4 minutes more.

options.label: Tender with a slight bite

media.alt: Correct rice: separate, tender, slight bite.
media.brief: Correct rice: separate, tender, slight bite.

options.guidance: Perfect. Take it off the heat now.

options.label: Soft and sticky

media.alt: Overcooked, sticky rice.
media.brief: Overcooked, sticky rice.

options.guidance: Spread it out thinly on the tray straight away to dry. Fry in smaller batches. It will still taste good.

steps.title: Spread the rice out to cool
steps.body: Spread the rice out in a thin layer on the tray and leave it to cool and dry. Fluff it with a fork once or twice.
steps.why: This is the secret. Warm, wet rice clumps and goes mushy when you fry it. Cooled, drier rice stays separate.

media.alt: Golden rice spread thin on a tray to cool.
media.brief: Golden rice spread thin on a tray to cool.

tips.text: Leftover rice from yesterday makes the best fried rice of all, because it’s already dry.

cues.see: A thin, even layer of yellow rice with steam rising off it at first, then none. The grains look dry and separate.
cues.texture: Cool and slightly firm to the touch, not sticky.

steps.title: Cook the prawns and liver
steps.body: Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in the big pan on medium-high. Add the diced liver and cook, stirring, until browned and no longer pink inside. Then add the prawns and cook until they turn pink and curl. Tip everything onto a plate.

cues.see: Prawns pink and curled into a “C” shape. A tight “O” shape means overcooked.

media.alt: Prawns turned pink and curled in the pan with browned liver.
media.brief: Prawns turned pink and curled in the pan with browned liver.

steps.title: Fry the vegetables quickly
steps.body: In the same pan, heat 1 tablespoon of oil and the butter on medium-high. Add the onion and garlic and stir for 1 minute. Add the carrots and green beans and stir-fry for 2 minutes. Add the peas, corn and green pepper and stir-fry for 1–2 minutes more. Season with a pinch of salt. Tip half of the vegetables into a bowl.

cues.see: Bright, shiny colours.
cues.texture: Still slightly crunchy. Not soft.

media.alt: 10-second clip: stir-frying the colourful vegetables on high heat.
media.brief: 10-second clip: stir-frying the colourful vegetables on high heat.

tips.text: Don’t let the vegetables go soft and dull. They’ll cook a little more with the rice.

steps.title: Fry the rice in two batches
steps.body: With half the vegetables still in the pan, add 1 tablespoon of oil and half the rice. Turn the heat up. Toss and stir-fry for 3–4 minutes, scraping from the bottom, until the rice is hot and every grain is coated. Sprinkle in half the white pepper and the second crumbled stock cube. Tip it into your serving dish. Repeat with the rest of the vegetables and rice.
steps.why: Too much rice at once steams instead of frying. Two batches keep it light and separate.

cues.hear: A lively crackle as the rice fries.
cues.see: Even golden colour, vegetables spread through every spoonful.

media.alt: 12-second clip: tossing golden rice and vegetables in a wide pan.
media.brief: 12-second clip: tossing golden rice and vegetables in a wide pan.

options.label: Patchy, white bits

media.alt: Fried rice with uneven colour.
media.brief: Fried rice with uneven colour.

options.guidance: Keep tossing for another minute. Add a pinch more curry powder if it looks pale.

options.label: Even gold, grains separate

media.alt: Correct fried rice: even gold, separate grains.
media.brief: Correct fried rice: even gold, separate grains.

options.guidance: Perfect.

options.label: Clumping together

media.alt: Clumpy fried rice.
media.brief: Clumpy fried rice.

options.guidance: Turn the heat up, press the clumps apart with the spatula and fry smaller amounts.

steps.title: Fold in the prawns, liver and spring onions
steps.body: Gently fold the prawns, liver and spring onions through all the rice. Taste and add salt if needed.

cues.see: Pink prawns, dark liver pieces and green spring onion spread evenly through golden rice.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve hot, on its own or with peppered chicken and dodo. For a true party plate, serve it half and half with jollof.

media.alt: Mcuire party plate: fried rice and jollof side by side, chicken, dodo, coleslaw.
media.brief: Mcuire party plate: fried rice and jollof side by side, chicken, dodo, coleslaw.

tips.text: Keeps 3 days in the fridge. Reheat in a hot pan with a splash of water, until steaming hot.

cues.see: Fluffy golden rice speckled with orange, green and yellow, every grain separate and shiny.

recipes.title: Coconut Rice
recipes.subtitle: Fragrant rice cooked in coconut milk with a gentle pepper base: rich, creamy and lightly sweet.
recipes.story: Coconut rice is jollof’s gentler cousin. The coconut milk makes every grain rich and fragrant. It’s cooked the same steam-not-boil way as jollof, but on even lower heat, because coconut milk catches on the bottom easily.
allergens: Coconut (classed as a tree nut in some countries)
Check stock cubes: some contain wheat, soy or celery
dietary: Gluten-free if your stock cubes are

hero.brief: Pale golden coconut rice in a pot, flecks of red pepper and thyme, toasted coconut on top. Overhead.

equipment.name: Heavy-bottomed pot with lid
equipment.note: Heavy is important. Coconut milk scorches in thin pots.

substitutes.name: Basmati rice
substitutes.note: Use ¼ less liquid and check 5 minutes earlier.

ingredients.name: Coconut milk (full-fat, tinned)

substitutes.name: Fresh coconut milk
substitutes.note: Grate 1 coconut, blend with 3 cups hot water and squeeze through a cloth.

ingredients.note: Full-fat gives the best flavour. Shake the tins first.

ingredients.name: Scotch bonnet peppers

substitutes.name: Habanero
substitutes.note: Same heat and fruity flavour.

ingredients.note: Use fewer, or remove the seeds, for less heat.

substitutes.name: Mild curry powder + pinch of turmeric
Bouillon powder
substitutes.note: 1 tsp per cube.

substitutes.name: Dried shrimp powder
substitutes.note: Asian grocery stores sell this. Same amount.

steps.title: Wash the rice and blend the pepper
steps.body: Wash the rice in a bowl of cold water 3–4 times until the water is mostly clear, then drain. Blend the red pepper, scotch bonnet and half the onion with 2 tablespoons of water until smooth. Slice the other half of the onion.

tips.text: Wash your hands with soap after cutting scotch bonnet, and keep them away from your eyes.

cues.see: Nearly clear rinse water, and a smooth orange-red pepper blend with no visible pieces.
cues.texture: The blend pours like a thin smoothie.

steps.title: Fry the pepper base
steps.body: Heat the oil in your pot on medium. Add the sliced onion and cook 2 minutes until soft. Pour in the pepper blend and fry, stirring often, until it thickens and darkens slightly.

cues.see: Thicker, deeper orange-red, a little oil at the edges.

media.alt: Pepper base fried in oil, thick and glossy.
media.brief: Pepper base fried in oil, thick and glossy.

steps.title: Add the coconut milk and season
steps.body: Pour in the coconut milk and the water or stock. Add the curry, thyme, bay leaves, crayfish (if using), stock cubes and salt. Stir and bring it just to a boil. Taste: it should be slightly saltier than you’d like, because the rice will absorb it.

media.alt: Creamy coconut sauce coming to the boil.
media.brief: Creamy coconut sauce coming to the boil.

cues.see: A creamy, pale orange liquid with small bubbles just breaking around the edge.
cues.smell: Sweet coconut with curry and thyme.
cues.hear: A gentle bubbling, not a roar.

steps.title: Add the rice and check the liquid
steps.body: Stir in the rice so every grain is coated, then press it flat. The liquid should sit just about half a centimetre above the rice: a little more than for jollof, because coconut milk is thicker.

media.alt: Rice pressed flat with coconut liquid just above it.
media.brief: Rice pressed flat with coconut liquid just above it.

options.label: Rice under lots of liquid

media.alt: Too much liquid over rice.
media.brief: Too much liquid over rice.

options.guidance: Spoon some out into a cup and keep it in case you need it later.

options.label: Just above the rice

media.alt: Correct liquid level.
media.brief: Correct liquid level.

options.guidance: Perfect.

options.label: Rice showing above the liquid

media.alt: Too little liquid.
media.brief: Too little liquid.

options.guidance: Add ¼ cup of water and press flat again.

cues.see: Rice lying flat under a thin layer of creamy liquid, about half a centimetre deep, like a shallow puddle.

steps.title: Cover tightly and steam on the lowest heat
steps.body: Cover with foil pressed around the rim, put the lid on and turn the heat to the lowest setting. Don’t open or stir.

media.alt: Pot covered with foil and lid on low flame.
media.brief: Pot covered with foil and lid on low flame.

tips.text: Coconut milk burns more easily than stock. If you smell any scorching, turn the heat even lower straight away.

cues.see: Foil sealed tight all around the rim, lid on top and the smallest flame you can make.
cues.hear: Very quiet. A soft crackle is fine; loud sizzling means the heat is too high.

steps.title: Check, fold and finish
steps.body: Taste a few grains. Gently fold the rice from the bottom with a flat spatula. Cover again and steam 10 more minutes on low.

media.alt: 8-second clip: folding coconut rice gently from the bottom.
media.brief: 8-second clip: folding coconut rice gently from the bottom.

options.label: Hard and dry

media.alt: Undercooked coconut rice.
media.brief: Undercooked coconut rice.

options.guidance: Sprinkle over ¼ cup of water, cover and steam 10 minutes more.

options.label: Soft, separate, creamy

media.alt: Perfect coconut rice.
media.brief: Perfect coconut rice.

options.guidance: Perfect. Turn off the heat.

options.label: Wet and sticky

media.alt: Wet coconut rice.
media.brief: Wet coconut rice.

options.guidance: Leave the lid off on the lowest heat for 5 minutes to dry out. Don’t stir.

cues.see: Pale golden grains, most of the liquid gone, a creamy film on the bottom.
cues.texture: Grains tender with a little bite in the centre before the last 10 minutes.

steps.title: Rest and serve
steps.body: Leave it covered off the heat for 5 minutes, remove the bay leaves and fluff with a fork. Scatter toasted coconut on top if you like.

media.alt: Mcuire plating: coconut rice with grilled fish and dodo.
media.brief: Mcuire plating: coconut rice with grilled fish and dodo.

cues.texture: Soft and slightly creamy, not sticky.

recipes.title: White Rice & Nigerian Tomato Stew
recipes.subtitle: Deep red, slow-fried tomato and pepper stew with chicken, over fluffy white rice.
recipes.story: This is the everyday meal of almost every Nigerian home, and the stew is a building block for dozens of other dishes. Learn it once and you’ll cook it for life. Like jollof, the secret is frying the pepper base slowly until the oil rises.
allergens: Check stock cubes: some contain wheat, soy or celery
dietary: Gluten-free if your stock cubes are

hero.brief: White rice with deep red Nigerian stew and a piece of fried chicken, on a Mcuire plate. 45°.

gallery.alt: A pot of finished stew with oil glistening on top and chicken pieces.
gallery.brief: A pot of finished stew with oil glistening on top and chicken pieces.

substitutes.name: Beef or goat
substitutes.note: Simmer 35–45 minutes in step 1 instead of 20.

ingredients.name: Red bell peppers (tatashe)
ingredients.note: These give the stew its deep red colour.

ingredients.name: Vegetable oil
ingredients.note: Nigerian stew is rich. The oil carries the flavour.

substitutes.name: Basmati or jasmine
substitutes.note: Use about 1 cup less water and check 5 minutes earlier.

steps.title: Season and cook the chicken
steps.body: Put the chicken in a pot with the half onion (sliced), 1 crumbled stock cube, a pinch of salt and ½ cup of water. Cover and cook on medium, turning once, until cooked through. Lift out the chicken and keep the liquid. It’s your stock.

cues.see: Chicken white all the way through, juices clear.

media.alt: Cooked chicken in golden stock.
media.brief: Cooked chicken in golden stock.

tips.text: Cut into the thickest piece by the bone. No pink, juices clear.

steps.title: Blend the stew base
steps.body: While the chicken cooks, blend the tomatoes, red peppers, scotch bonnets and one onion until smooth.

media.alt: Smooth red stew base in a blender.
media.brief: Smooth red stew base in a blender.

cues.see: A smooth, bright orange-red blend with no chunks of pepper skin.
cues.texture: Like a thin smoothie.

steps.title: Boil the base down until thick
steps.body: Pour the blend into a pot and cook uncovered on medium-high, stirring every few minutes, until about half the water has gone and it looks thick.

cues.texture: Like a loose porridge. A spoon leaves a trail.

media.alt: Stew base reduced by half, thick and darker.
media.brief: Stew base reduced by half, thick and darker.

tips.text: It splutters. Tilt the lid over the pot, leaving a gap.

media.alt: Thin stew base.
media.brief: Thin stew base.

options.label: Thick, spoon leaves a trail

media.brief: Thick stew base.

steps.title: Fry the chicken (optional)
steps.body: For extra flavour, fry the cooked chicken in 3 tablespoons of the oil in a frying pan on medium-high until golden on both sides. Skip this if you prefer. The stew is still delicious.

media.alt: Golden fried chicken pieces in a pan.
media.brief: Golden fried chicken pieces in a pan.

cues.see: Golden-brown skin on both sides of each chicken piece.
cues.hear: A steady sizzle. Spitting means the chicken is still wet: pat it dry.

steps.title: Fry the onion and tomato paste
steps.body: Heat the rest of the oil in your big pot on medium. Add the sliced onion and cook for 3 minutes. Add the tomato paste and stir almost constantly until it turns from bright red to a deeper brick red.

cues.see: Deeper brick red.

media.alt: Tomato paste fried to brick red with onions.
media.brief: Tomato paste fried to brick red with onions.

steps.title: Fry the stew base until the oil rises
steps.body: Add the thick stew base, bay leaves, thyme and curry. Fry on medium, stirring every 2–3 minutes and scraping the bottom, until it’s deep red and the oil floats on top.
steps.why: Frying the base slowly is what makes Nigerian stew taste rich and sweet instead of sour.

steps.title: Cook the white rice
steps.body: Wash the rice 3–4 times until the water is mostly clear. Put it in a pot with the water and a pinch of salt. Bring to the boil, then cover, turn the heat to low and cook until the water is absorbed and the rice is soft.

options.guidance: Turn off the heat and keep it covered.

steps.title: Add stock and chicken, then simmer
steps.body: Pour about 1 cup of the chicken stock into the stew. Add 2 crumbled stock cubes and stir. Add the chicken, cover and simmer on low so the chicken soaks up the stew. Taste and add salt if needed.

media.alt: Chicken pieces simmering in red stew.
media.brief: Chicken pieces simmering in red stew.

tips.text: Thick enough to coat a spoon, deep red, with a little oil on top. It tastes rich and slightly sweet.

cues.see: A deep red stew bubbling gently around the chicken, with a thin layer of red oil at the edges.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Remove the bay leaves. Spoon the rice onto plates, ladle stew over it and add a piece of chicken. It’s even better with dodo on the side.

media.alt: Mcuire plating: white rice, red stew, chicken and dodo.
media.brief: Mcuire plating: white rice, red stew, chicken and dodo.

tips.text: Stew keeps 4 days in the fridge and 3 months in the freezer. Many families cook a big pot on Sunday for the whole week.

cues.see: Fluffy white rice with a ladle of deep red, glossy stew on one side and a piece of chicken on top.

recipes.title: Ofada Rice with Ayamase
recipes.subtitle: Nutty local rice with the famous green-pepper “designer stew”, rich with iru and assorted meat.
recipes.story: Ofada is an aromatic, unpolished Nigerian rice. Ayamase is its partner: a fiery green-pepper stew fried slowly in palm oil with iru. It’s bold, smoky and unforgettable. We’ll show you the traditional palm-oil method safely, plus an easier option.
allergens: Eggs
Fish and shellfish (crayfish)
Check stock cubes: some contain wheat, soy or celery
dietary: Gluten-free if your stock cubes are

hero.brief: Ofada rice on a green uma leaf with dark green ayamase stew, boiled eggs and assorted meat. 45°.

equipment.name: Two pots
equipment.note: One for rice, one for the stew.

equipment.name: Sieve
equipment.note: For draining the pepper blend and rinsing rice.

ingredients.name: Ofada rice

substitutes.name: Brown basmati or short-grain brown rice
substitutes.note: Not the same aroma, but a good nutty match.

ingredients.note: Short, unpolished and fragrant. It often contains small stones: always pick through it.

substitutes.name: Smoked turkey wings
substitutes.note: Popular in Canada and the US. Simmer about 40 minutes.

ingredients.name: Green scotch bonnet or habanero peppers

substitutes.name: Habanero
substitutes.note: Same heat and fruity flavour.

ingredients.note: Ayamase is meant to be hot. Use 2 for a milder stew.

ingredients.name: Red palm oil

substitutes.name: Vegetable oil + 1 tsp sweet paprika
substitutes.note: Right colour, milder flavour. Use it only if you can’t find palm oil.

ingredients.note: Gives the colour and the true taste. It may be solid in a cold kitchen. That’s normal.

substitutes.name: 1 tsp white miso
substitutes.note: Similar fermented depth.

substitutes.name: Dried shrimp powder
substitutes.note: Asian grocery stores sell this. Same amount.

substitutes.name: Bouillon powder
substitutes.note: 1 tsp per cube.

steps.title: Season and cook the meat
steps.body: Put the meat in your pot with a little chopped onion, 1 crumbled stock cube, a pinch of salt and ½ cup of water. Cover and let it steam in its own juices for 10 minutes. Then add enough water to just cover it and simmer until tender. Keep the liquid. It’s your stock.

cues.texture: A fork slides into the meat easily.

media.alt: Seasoned meat simmering in its own stock.
media.brief: Seasoned meat simmering in its own stock.

tips.text: Never pour this stock away. It carries flavour into the whole soup.

steps.title: Pick and wash the ofada rice
steps.body: Spread the rice on a tray and pick out any stones or dark grains. Then wash it in plenty of water, rubbing it between your hands, 4–5 times until the water runs clearer.

media.alt: Ofada rice spread on a tray, small stones picked out.
media.brief: Ofada rice spread on a tray, small stones picked out.

tips.text: Don’t skip picking. A stone in ofada can break a tooth.

cues.see: No stones or black grains left on the tray, and the rinse water runs much clearer.
cues.smell: Ofada rice smells earthy, almost like hay. That’s normal and part of its charm.

steps.title: Par-boil, rinse, then cook the rice
steps.body: Boil the rice in plenty of water for 10 minutes, then drain and rinse it. Return it to the pot with fresh water about 2 cm above the rice and a pinch of salt. Cover and cook on low until tender.
steps.why: The first boil washes away the strong starchy smell, so the rice tastes nutty, not musty.

options.label: Still chalky

media.alt: Undercooked ofada.
media.brief: Undercooked ofada.

options.guidance: Add a splash of water and cook 5–10 minutes more. Ofada stays slightly chewy even when done.

options.label: Tender with a little chew

media.alt: Cooked ofada rice.
media.brief: Cooked ofada rice.

options.guidance: Perfect. Turn off and keep covered.

cues.see: Plump, reddish-brown grains with a few split open.
cues.texture: Tender but still a little chewy. Ofada is never soft like white rice.

steps.title: Blend the green peppers roughly, then drain
steps.body: Remove the seeds from the bell peppers. Blend them with the scotch bonnets and one onion for just a few seconds: it should be coarse. Pour into a sieve and let the watery juice drain away for a few minutes.
steps.why: Draining the water shortens the frying time and keeps the stew thick and rich.

media.alt: Coarse green pepper blend draining in a sieve.
media.brief: Coarse green pepper blend draining in a sieve.

tips.text: Wash your hands with soap after cutting scotch bonnet, and keep them away from your eyes.

cues.see: A coarse, bright green blend with small visible pieces, and clear-ish juice dripping out of the sieve.
cues.texture: Thick and grainy, like a chunky salsa.

steps.title: Bleach the palm oil (or take the easy way)
steps.body:
Traditional ayamase uses “bleached” palm oil for its smoky taste. Open a window and turn on your extractor fan. Heat the palm oil in a dry pot with the lid slightly ajar on medium heat until it turns from deep red to pale and clear. Then turn the heat OFF and let it cool for 5 minutes before you continue.

Easy way: skip bleaching and use half palm oil, half vegetable oil. It’s still delicious, just less smoky.

media.alt: Bleached palm oil: pale, clear yellow in the pot.
media.brief: Bleached palm oil: pale, clear yellow in the pot.

tips.text: Bleaching makes smoke. Never leave the pot, keep the lid nearby, and never add ingredients to oil that’s still smoking hot: they will splatter violently.

options.label: Still deep red

media.alt: Palm oil still red.
media.brief: Palm oil still red.

options.guidance: Keep heating, a few minutes more.

options.label: Pale and clear

media.alt: Bleached palm oil, pale.
media.brief: Bleached palm oil, pale.

options.guidance: Turn off the heat and let it cool for 5 minutes.

options.label: Smoking heavily

media.alt: Heavy smoke from oil.
media.brief: Heavy smoke from oil.

options.guidance: Turn off the heat now, put the lid on and move the pot off the burner. Let it cool fully before continuing.

cues.see: The oil goes from deep red to pale gold and almost clear.
cues.smell: Smoky. Some smoke is expected. Open the window and keep the fan on.
cues.hear: A light crackle as the oil heats. Turn off the heat before you add anything.

steps.title: Fry the iru and onion
steps.body: Put the cooled oil back on medium-low. Add the sliced onion and the iru and stir for 2 minutes.

steps.title: Fry the green peppers slowly
steps.body: Add the drained pepper blend. Fry on medium-low, stirring every few minutes, until the water has gone, the peppers darken to olive green and the oil separates.

cues.see: Olive green peppers sitting in clear oil.
cues.smell: Roasted pepper, no longer raw or grassy.

media.alt: Ayamase frying: olive-green peppers with oil separated.
media.brief: Ayamase frying: olive-green peppers with oil separated.

options.label: Bright green and watery

media.alt: Raw-looking green pepper mix.
media.brief: Raw-looking green pepper mix.

options.guidance: Keep frying. This step takes patience.

options.label: Olive green, oil separated

media.alt: Correctly fried ayamase.
media.brief: Correctly fried ayamase.

options.guidance: Perfect. Add the meat.

steps.title: Add meat, eggs and seasoning
steps.body: Add the cooked meat, the boiled eggs, the crayfish, the stock cubes and a splash of meat stock. Stir gently and fry together for 10 minutes so the meat soaks up the stew. Taste and add salt.

media.alt: Ayamase with assorted meat and eggs.
media.brief: Ayamase with assorted meat and eggs.

cues.see: Dark olive-green stew coating the meat and eggs, with oil rising around the edges.
cues.smell: Smoky, peppery and savoury from the iru and crayfish.

steps.title: Serve the Mcuire way
steps.body: Serve the ofada rice with the ayamase spooned beside it, plus an egg and plenty of meat. If you can find uma leaves (sold frozen at African groceries), line the plate with them. That’s how it’s served in Lagos.

media.alt: Ofada and ayamase served on uma leaves.
media.brief: Ofada and ayamase served on uma leaves.

cues.see: Brown ofada rice on a green leaf, the dark green ayamase beside it, an egg and plenty of meat.

recipes.title: Waakye
recipes.subtitle: Ghana’s beloved rice and beans, cooked with sorghum leaves for its deep wine-red colour.
recipes.story: Waakye (say “waa-chay”) is Ghana’s favourite breakfast and lunch. Rice and beans cook together with dried sorghum leaves, which turn everything a beautiful reddish-brown. It’s served with a spread of extras, and shito pepper sauce is a must.

hero.brief: Reddish-brown waakye with shito, a boiled egg, fried plantain and a sprinkle of gari. Overhead.

gallery.alt: Dried waakye (sorghum) leaves next to the deep red cooking water.
gallery.brief: Dried waakye (sorghum) leaves next to the deep red cooking water.

substitutes.name: Parboiled rice
substitutes.note: Add 5 minutes and a little more water.

ingredients.name: Dried waakye leaves (sorghum leaves)

substitutes.name: ¼ tsp baking soda
substitutes.note: Gives a brown colour (not as red). Some Ghanaian cooks add a pinch anyway to soften the beans.

ingredients.note: They give the colour. They are removed before serving.

steps.title: Soak the beans
steps.body: Cover the beans with plenty of water and soak them. This makes them cook faster and more evenly.

tips.text: Soaking overnight is easiest: start it before bed.

cues.see: The beans swell to about twice their size and the skins look smooth and full.

steps.title: Boil the beans with the leaves
steps.body: Drain the beans. Rinse the waakye leaves and tie them in a bundle (or leave them loose). Put the beans and leaves in your pot with 6 cups of water. Boil, then simmer with the lid partly on until the beans are almost tender.

cues.see: The water turns a deep wine-red.
cues.texture: A bean squashes between your fingers but is still firm in the middle.

media.alt: Beans boiling with sorghum leaves, water deep wine-red.
media.brief: Beans boiling with sorghum leaves, water deep wine-red.

checkpoint.question: Squash a bean. How is it?

options.label: Hard all through

media.alt: Hard bean.
media.brief: Hard bean.

options.guidance: Keep simmering, check every 10 minutes. Add water if it gets low.

options.label: Squashes, firm middle

media.alt: Almost-tender bean.
media.brief: Almost-tender bean.

options.guidance: Perfect timing to add the rice. It will finish cooking with the rice.

options.label: Already very soft

media.alt: Very soft beans.
media.brief: Very soft beans.

options.guidance: Fine! Just stir gently from now on so they don’t turn to mush.

steps.title: Wash the rice
steps.body: Wash the rice 3–4 times until the water is mostly clear and drain it.

cues.see: The rinse water goes from cloudy to mostly clear.

steps.title: Add the rice and cook together
steps.body: Add the rice and salt to the beans and red water. Stir once. The water should be about 2 cm above the rice; add more if needed. Bring to the boil, then cover, turn to low and cook until the water is absorbed.

media.alt: Rice and beans cooking together in red water.
media.brief: Rice and beans cooking together in red water.

cues.see: Reddish-brown water about 2 cm above the rice, and the beans spread through it.
cues.hear: A steady boil, then almost silent once the lid is on and the heat is low.

steps.title: Check, remove the leaves and rest
steps.body: Taste the rice and a few beans. Both should be soft. Remove the leaves, fluff gently with a fork, cover and rest for 5 minutes.

options.label: Reddish-brown, soft rice and beans

media.alt: Perfect waakye colour and texture.
media.brief: Perfect waakye colour and texture.

options.guidance: That’s waakye.

options.label: Pale colour

media.alt: Pale waakye.
media.brief: Pale waakye.

options.guidance: Still tasty. Next time use a few more leaves and let the beans simmer with them longer.

cues.see: Reddish-brown rice and beans with no water left at the bottom.
cues.texture: Both the rice and the beans are soft all the way through.

steps.title: Serve with all the extras
steps.body: Serve waakye with shito (Ghanaian black pepper sauce), a boiled egg, fried plantain and a sprinkle of gari. Spaghetti, avocado and fried fish are popular extras too.

media.alt: Mcuire waakye plate with all the classic sides.
media.brief: Mcuire waakye plate with all the classic sides.

tips.text: Shito is sold in jars at most African grocery stores. It’s the one extra you shouldn’t skip.

cues.see: Reddish-brown waakye with dark shito, a white egg, golden plantain and a sprinkle of pale gari.

recipes.title: Thiéboudienne
recipes.subtitle: Senegal’s national dish: herb-stuffed fish and vegetables, with broken rice cooked in the rich tomato broth.
recipes.story: Thiéboudienne (say “cheb-oo-jen”) means “rice and fish” in Wolof. Fish stuffed with a green herb paste and vegetables simmer in a tomato broth, and then the rice cooks in that same broth. Everything comes to the table on one big shared platter.
allergens: Fish
Check stock cubes: some contain wheat, soy or celery
dietary: Gluten-free if your stock cubes are

hero.brief: A large platter of red broken rice topped with stuffed fish steaks, carrots, cassava, cabbage and lime. Overhead.

serveWith: Extra hot pepper on the side

ingredients.name: Firm white fish steaks (grouper, sea bass or snapper)

substitutes.name: Cod or haddock steaks
substitutes.note: More delicate: cook them for less time in step 5.

ingredients.note: Ask for thick steaks, bone-in.

ingredients.name: Scotch bonnet peppers

substitutes.name: Habanero
substitutes.note: Same heat and fruity flavour.

ingredients.note: Use fewer, or remove the seeds, for less heat.

ingredients.name: Broken rice

substitutes.name: Jasmine rice, pulsed briefly in a blender
substitutes.note: Or just use whole jasmine rice.

ingredients.note: Sold as “broken jasmine rice” in Asian grocery stores.

ingredients.name: Pumpkin or butternut squash, in chunks

substitutes.name: Bouillon powder
substitutes.note: 1 tsp per cube.

steps.title: Make the rof (green herb paste)
steps.body: Blend or pound the parsley, garlic, spring onions, scotch bonnet, black pepper and a teaspoon of salt into a thick green paste.

media.alt: Bright green rof paste in a mortar.
media.brief: Bright green rof paste in a mortar.

tips.text: Wash your hands with soap after cutting scotch bonnet, and keep them away from your eyes.

steps.title: Stuff the fish
steps.body: Cut two or three deep slits in each fish steak. Push a little rof into each slit with your finger. Keep a spoonful of rof for the broth.

media.alt: 10-second clip: pushing green rof paste into slits in a fish steak.
media.brief: 10-second clip: pushing green rof paste into slits in a fish steak.

cues.see: Two or three deep slits in each steak, each one packed with bright green rof.

steps.title: Brown the fish
steps.body: Heat the oil in your big pot on medium-high. Fry the fish for about 3 minutes on each side, until golden. It doesn’t need to cook through. Lift it out onto a plate.

media.alt: Fish steaks browning in oil.
media.brief: Fish steaks browning in oil.

tips.text: Don’t move the fish while it browns. It releases from the pot when it’s ready to turn.

cues.see: A golden crust on both sides. The middle can still look raw.
cues.hear: A loud, steady sizzle as the fish goes in.

steps.title: Make the tomato base
steps.body: In the same oil, cook the sliced onions for 3 minutes. Stir in the tomato paste with ½ cup of water and fry, stirring, until it darkens to a deep brick red.

media.alt: Deep red tomato base with onions.
media.brief: Deep red tomato base with onions.

cues.see: The onions soften, then the paste darkens from bright red to deep brick red and the oil turns red.

steps.title: Simmer the vegetables, then the fish
steps.body: Add 8 cups of water, the stock cubes, bay leaves and the leftover rof. Bring to a boil. Add the cassava, carrots and cabbage and simmer for 15 minutes. Then add the fish, pumpkin, eggplant and okra and simmer 15 minutes more, until everything is tender.

media.alt: Vegetables and fish simmering in red broth.
media.brief: Vegetables and fish simmering in red broth.

cues.see: A red-orange broth full of vegetables. Cassava and carrots are tender when a knife slides in easily.

steps.title: Lift out the fish and vegetables
steps.body: Carefully lift the fish and vegetables into a bowl. Ladle a little broth over them and cover to keep them warm and moist. Measure what’s left in the pot: you need about 5 cups of broth for the rice. Add water or remove broth to get there.

cues.see: Fish and vegetables in a covered bowl, and about 5 cups of red broth left in the pot.

steps.title: Cook the rice in the broth
steps.body: Wash the broken rice, then stir it into the simmering broth. Cover tightly, turn to low and cook until the rice has absorbed the broth.

cues.see: Deep orange-red rice.
cues.texture: Soft and fluffy, each little grain separate.

media.alt: Broken rice cooked red in the broth.
media.brief: Broken rice cooked red in the broth.

tips.text: The crispy layer at the bottom is called xooñ (“hon”). It’s the cook’s treat, so share it with whoever helped.

options.label: Still hard, pot dry

media.alt: Dry, underdone broken rice.
media.brief: Dry, underdone broken rice.

options.guidance: Add ½ cup of reserved broth, cover and cook 10 minutes more.

options.label: Soft, fluffy, red

media.alt: Perfect thiéboudienne rice.
media.brief: Perfect thiéboudienne rice.

options.guidance: Perfect.

steps.title: Build the platter
steps.body: Spread the rice over a large platter. Arrange the fish in the middle and the vegetables around it. Add lime wedges. In Senegal everyone eats from the same platter, each from their own side.

media.alt: Mcuire thiéboudienne platter, fish centre, vegetables around, lime.
media.brief: Mcuire thiéboudienne platter, fish centre, vegetables around, lime.

cues.see: Red broken rice spread over a big platter, the fish in the centre and colourful vegetables all around, with lime wedges.

recipes.title: Egusi Soup
recipes.subtitle: Golden lumps of fried melon seed in a rich palm-oil soup with tender meat and greens.
recipes.story: Egusi is the soup most people fall in love with first. The secret at Mcuire is frying the egusi paste in palm oil before any liquid goes in. That gives you soft, nutty lumps instead of a grainy soup. We’ll show you exactly what each stage looks like, so you know you’ve got it right.
allergens: Fish and shellfish (dried fish, crayfish)
Check stock cubes: some contain wheat, soy or celery
dietary: Gluten-free if your stock cubes are

hero.brief: Finished egusi in a clay pot: golden lumps, glossy red oil on top, green leaves through it, meat visible. Overhead.

gallery.alt: Plated: egusi beside a smooth ball of pounded yam on a Mcuire plate. 45°.
gallery.brief: Plated: egusi beside a smooth ball of pounded yam on a Mcuire plate. 45°.

gallery.alt: Close-up of the egusi lumps, showing their soft, crumbly texture.
gallery.brief: Close-up of the egusi lumps, showing their soft, crumbly texture.

steps.title: Set out everything you need
steps.body: Wash your hands. Put the meat in a bowl and rinse it under cold water, then drain. Peel the onions. Chop one onion finely and cut the other into quarters. Wash the greens in a colander, shake them dry and chop them roughly.

media.alt: All egusi ingredients on the Mcuire counter: ground egusi, palm oil, crayfish, meat, fish, peppers, greens.
media.brief: All egusi ingredients on the Mcuire counter: ground egusi, palm oil, crayfish, meat, fish, peppers, greens.

tips.text: Wash the greens in two changes of water. Spinach and ugu often hide grit, and nobody wants crunchy soup.

cues.see: Rinsed meat in a bowl, one onion finely chopped and one in quarters, and a pile of roughly chopped greens.

steps.title: Season the meat and let it steam
steps.body: Put the meat (and assorted meat, if using) in your big pot. Add two of the onion quarters, 1 crumbled stock cube, half the salt and ½ cup of water. Stir, cover with the lid and cook on medium heat. The meat will release its own juices and soak up the seasoning.
steps.why: Steaming meat in its own juices first gives it far more flavour than boiling it in lots of water.

cues.smell: After a few minutes, a rich savoury smell.
cues.see: The meat turns from red to grey-brown and juices collect at the bottom.

media.alt: Seasoned raw beef chunks in the pot with onion quarters, before the lid goes on.
media.brief: Seasoned raw beef chunks in the pot with onion quarters, before the lid goes on.

tips.text: If the pot starts to sizzle and stick, add a few tablespoons of water. It should steam, not fry.

steps.title: Simmer the meat until tender
steps.body: Add 3 cups of water, cover again and let it bubble gently on medium-low heat until the meat is tender. Meanwhile, do the next few steps.

cues.texture: A fork slides into a piece of meat easily. Goat may take longer than beef.

tips.text: Don’t throw this liquid away. It’s your stock, and it’s full of flavour. You’ll pour it into the soup later.
Check now and then. If the water drops below the meat, add another cup.

options.label: The fork pushes back

media.alt: Fork pressing into firm beef that resists.
media.brief: Fork pressing into firm beef that resists.

options.guidance: Keep simmering and check every 10 minutes. Add water if the pot is getting low.

options.label: The fork slides in

media.alt: Fork sliding easily into a tender beef chunk.
media.brief: Fork sliding easily into a tender beef chunk.

options.guidance: Perfect. Turn off the heat. Keep the meat in its stock for now.

steps.title: Prepare the dried fish
steps.body: While the meat cooks, put the dried fish in a bowl and cover it with hot water from the kettle. Leave it for 10 minutes to soften. Then lift it out, pull off any hard bones and skin with your fingers, and break the fish into bite-size pieces.

media.alt: Softened dried fish being broken into pieces by hand, bones set aside.
media.brief: Softened dried fish being broken into pieces by hand, bones set aside.

tips.text: Soaking also washes off any sand or dust, so drain away that water.

cues.see: The dried fish goes from hard and stiff to soft and flaky. The water turns cloudy and brown.
cues.smell: Strong and smoky. That smell becomes the soup’s depth.

steps.title: Blend the peppers
steps.body: Put the scotch bonnets, red bell pepper and the remaining two onion quarters into the blender with 3 tablespoons of water. Blend for just a few seconds. You want it a little coarse, not a smooth juice.

cues.see: A rough, orange-red mix with tiny visible bits.

media.alt: Blender jug with a coarse pepper and onion blend.
media.brief: Blender jug with a coarse pepper and onion blend.

tips.text: Wash your hands with soap after touching scotch bonnet, and keep them away from your eyes.

steps.title: Mix the egusi into a thick paste
steps.body: Put the ground egusi in a bowl. Add ½ cup of water a little at a time, stirring with a spoon, until it becomes one thick paste that holds together.
steps.why: A thick paste is what turns into soft lumps when it fries. Too much water and it melts into the soup instead.

cues.texture: Like thick peanut butter. It holds its shape on the spoon.

media.alt: 8-second clip: stirring water into ground egusi until it forms a thick paste that holds on the spoon.
media.brief: 8-second clip: stirring water into ground egusi until it forms a thick paste that holds on the spoon.

media.brief: Egusi with too little water: dry crumbs.

options.label: Thick paste, holds its shape

media.alt: Correct egusi paste: thick, holding shape on a spoon.
media.brief: Correct egusi paste: thick, holding shape on a spoon.

options.guidance: Exactly right.

media.brief: Egusi with too much water: loose and runny.

steps.title: Warm the palm oil and soften the onion
steps.body: Lift the meat out of its stock into a bowl and pour the stock into a jug. Wipe the pot dry. Put it back on medium heat and add the palm oil. When the oil has melted and looks clear and bright red, add the chopped onion and the iru (if using). Stir for 2 minutes.

steps.title: Fry the egusi into lumps
steps.body: Drop the egusi paste into the oil in spoonfuls, spread around the pot. Now leave it alone for 3–4 minutes. Don’t stir. Then gently turn the pieces over with your spatula. Keep frying on medium-low, turning every couple of minutes, until the lumps look drier and golden and the oil is red and clear around them.
steps.why: This is the Mcuire secret. Frying the paste first gives soft, nutty lumps instead of a grainy soup.

cues.smell: Nutty and toasty, like roasted seeds.

steps.body: Taste a spoonful (let it cool first). Add salt a pinch at a time, or the last stock cube, until it tastes rich and savoury. If it needs more heat, add a little extra pepper now.

recipes.title: Ogbono Soup
recipes.subtitle: The famously “drawy” soup: silky, savoury and stretchy, perfect with swallow.
recipes.story: Ogbono is made from ground wild mango seeds. When cooked, they give the soup its famous “draw”: long, silky strands when you lift your spoon. The key is low heat and patience. Rush it and it burns or goes lumpy.
allergens: Fish and shellfish (dried fish, crayfish)

steps.title: Add the spices and seasoning
steps.body: Add the banga spice, scotch bonnet, crayfish, chopped onion, dried fish, meat (if using) and stock cubes. Simmer for 5 minutes.

cues.see: A rich, red-orange soup with spice flecks.
cues.smell: Banga spice is warm and aromatic, a little like aniseed and wood.

steps.title: Add the fresh fish
steps.body: Lower the fish steaks into the soup. Simmer gently for 10 minutes without stirring. Swirl the pot instead, so the fish stays whole.

media.alt: Fish steaks in banga soup.
media.brief: Fish steaks in banga soup.

steps.title: Finish with scent leaves
steps.body: Add the sliced scent leaves, taste and add salt. Turn off the heat.

cues.see: Thin green strips of scent leaf over a thick, deep red-orange soup.
cues.smell: Fresh, minty-basil scent leaf on top of the palm fruit.

steps.title: Serve with swallow
steps.body: Serve hot in deep bowls with your swallow (eba, pounded yam, fufu or semolina). Pinch off a small piece of swallow, roll it, make a dent with your thumb and scoop up the soup.

media.alt: Mcuire plating: the soup in a bowl beside a smooth ball of swallow.

recipes.title: Pounded Yam
recipes.subtitle: Smooth, stretchy and soft: the king of swallows, made in a modern kitchen.
recipes.story: Pounded yam is traditionally beaten in a big wooden mortar, and it’s hard work. At home a food processor or stand mixer does the pounding for you. The secret is the same either way: work the yam while it’s very hot.

hero.brief: Two smooth, glossy white balls of pounded yam beside a bowl of egusi. 45°.

gallery.alt: A whole puna yam next to peeled white chunks.
gallery.brief: A whole puna yam next to peeled white chunks.

equipment.name: Food processor or stand mixer (paddle)
equipment.note: Or a traditional mortar and pestle.

equipment.name: Kitchen gloves
equipment.note: Raw yam can make some people’s hands itch.

ingredients.name: Puna yam (African white yam)
ingredients.note: A big, rough, brown tuber. Sweet potatoes and “yams” from mainstream North American supermarkets are not the same and won’t work.

substitutes.name: Pounded yam flour (poundo yam)
substitutes.note: About 2 cups for 4 people. Make it like eba (see the Eba lesson): water first, flour on top, then turn until smooth.

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.note: Enough to cover the yam.

steps.title: Peel and cut the yam
steps.body: Put on gloves if you have them. Cut the yam into thick rounds, about 4 cm. Stand each round flat and cut away the brown skin with your knife, along with any pink or brown spots underneath. Cut the white flesh into chunks about 4 cm. Rinse them and keep them in a bowl of cold water.
steps.why: Equal chunks cook evenly. Keeping them in water stops them turning grey.

media.alt: 15-second clip: cutting a yam into rounds and peeling with a knife.
media.brief: 15-second clip: cutting a yam into rounds and peeling with a knife.

tips.text: Raw yam is slippery and the skin is tough. Always cut away from your hand on a board that doesn’t slide.

cues.see: Clean, bright white chunks with no brown skin or pink spots, waiting in cold water.

steps.title: Boil until very soft
steps.body: Put the yam in a pot, cover with water and bring to the boil. Cook on medium-high with the lid partly on until the yam is very soft.

cues.texture: A fork slides straight through and the edges begin to crumble.

media.alt: Boiled yam chunks, edges softening and slightly crumbly.
media.brief: Boiled yam chunks, edges softening and slightly crumbly.

options.label: Firm in the middle

media.alt: Yam with a firm, raw-looking centre.
media.brief: Yam with a firm, raw-looking centre.

options.guidance: Keep boiling and check every 5 minutes. Any hard bits will become lumps later.

options.label: Fork slides through, edges crumbling

media.alt: Correctly boiled yam, fork sliding through.
media.brief: Correctly boiled yam, fork sliding through.

options.guidance: Perfect. Move quickly to the next step while it’s hot.

steps.title: Drain, keeping a little water
steps.body: Scoop out 1 cup of the hot cooking water into a mug and keep it nearby. Drain the rest of the water away.

cues.see: A mug of cloudy, starchy cooking water by the stove, and steaming hot yam in the pot.

steps.title: Pound it while it’s hot
steps.body:
Working quickly, put half the hot yam into the food processor (or stand mixer bowl). Pulse a few times to break it up, then run it for 1–2 minutes. Add 1–2 tablespoons of the hot water if it gets stuck. Stop when it’s one smooth, stretchy ball. Repeat with the rest.

Using a mortar? Pound the hot yam with the pestle, turning it over with a wet wooden spoon, until smooth.
steps.why: Yam only becomes stretchy while it’s hot. Once it cools it turns lumpy and gluey.

cues.texture: Smooth, soft, slightly sticky and stretchy, like a soft dough.
cues.see: Glossy white, with no lumps.

media.alt: 20-second clip: hot yam in a food processor turning into a smooth, stretchy ball.
media.brief: 20-second clip: hot yam in a food processor turning into a smooth, stretchy ball.

tips.text: Speed matters more than strength. Have the processor ready before you drain the yam.

options.label: Lumpy and crumbly

media.alt: Lumpy pounded yam with visible bits.
media.brief: Lumpy pounded yam with visible bits.

options.guidance: Add 1–2 tablespoons of the hot water and process for another minute.

options.label: Smooth and stretchy

media.alt: Correct pounded yam: smooth, stretchy, glossy.
media.brief: Correct pounded yam: smooth, stretchy, glossy.

options.guidance: Perfect pounded yam.

options.label: Very soft and gluey

media.brief: Over-wet pounded yam, too soft.

options.guidance: A little too much water. It’s still fine to eat. Next time, add water only a spoonful at a time.

steps.title: Shape and serve
steps.body: Wet a wooden spoon or your hands with water. Scoop out portions and shape them into smooth balls. Serve straight away with soup, or wrap each one in cling film to keep it warm and soft.

media.alt: Shaped balls of pounded yam, some wrapped in cling film.
media.brief: Shaped balls of pounded yam, some wrapped in cling film.

tips.text: Wrapped pounded yam stays soft for about an hour. Leftovers can be reheated in the microwave, still wrapped, for 1 minute.

cues.see: Smooth, glossy white balls with no cracks or lumps.
cues.texture: Soft and stretchy, like a smooth dough that springs back.

recipes.title: Eba
recipes.subtitle: The quickest swallow there is: smooth, soft garri you can shape and dip in any soup.
recipes.story: Eba is made from garri, which is toasted cassava. It takes five minutes and only two ingredients, but getting it smooth with no lumps is a skill. We’ll show you the feel you’re looking for.

hero.brief: Two smooth, shaped balls of yellow eba on a plate next to a bowl of soup. 45°.

gallery.alt: Yellow garri and white garri side by side in small bowls.
gallery.brief: Yellow garri and white garri side by side in small bowls.

equipment.name: Wooden spoon or turning stick
equipment.note: A strong, flat wooden spoon is best.

equipment.name: Cling film
equipment.note: Optional, for wrapping and keeping it warm.

ingredients.name: Garri (yellow or white)
ingredients.note: Yellow garri has palm oil in it and tastes slightly richer. White is milder. Fine garri gives the smoothest eba.

substitutes.name: Fine semolina
substitutes.note: Makes a different swallow (semolina). Cook it in a pot. See the Semolina lesson.

ingredients.name: Boiling water
ingredients.note: It must be boiling, not just hot.

steps.title: Boil the water
steps.body: Boil the water in a kettle or pot until it’s at a full, rolling boil with big bubbles.
steps.why: Boiling water cooks the garri properly. Warm water gives you raw-tasting, sandy eba.

cues.hear: The kettle clicks off, or the pot bubbles hard.

tips.text: Boiling water burns. Keep the bowl on a stable, flat surface and keep children away.

steps.title: Pour water in first, then sprinkle the garri
steps.body: Pour about two-thirds of the boiling water into the bowl (keep the rest nearby). Now sprinkle the garri evenly over the top of the water, a handful at a time, until the garri covers the water and you can’t see any water through it. Don’t stir yet.

cues.see: A layer of garri sitting on top of the water, slowly getting darker as it soaks.

media.alt: 10-second clip: sprinkling garri evenly over hot water until it covers the surface.
media.brief: 10-second clip: sprinkling garri evenly over hot water until it covers the surface.

tips.text: Water first, garri on top. This is how we avoid lumps: every grain gets wet at the same time.

steps.title: Let it soak
steps.body: Leave the bowl alone so the garri can soak up the water and swell.

cues.see: The garri swells and the water disappears.

steps.title: Turn the eba until smooth
steps.body: Hold the bowl steady with one hand (use a cloth, as it’s hot). With the wooden spoon, press the garri firmly against the side of the bowl, then fold it over onto itself. Press, fold, turn the bowl a little, and repeat. Keep going until it comes together in one smooth piece.

cues.texture: Smooth, soft and slightly stretchy, like playdough. It holds its shape when you stop.

media.alt: 20-second clip: pressing and folding eba against the bowl with a wooden spoon until smooth.
media.brief: 20-second clip: pressing and folding eba against the bowl with a wooden spoon until smooth.

tips.text: Use your strength. Turning eba is pressing and folding, not stirring in circles.

options.label: Too soft and sticky

media.alt: Eba too soft: sticky, not holding shape.
media.brief: Eba too soft: sticky, not holding shape.

options.guidance: Sprinkle in 1–2 more tablespoons of garri and keep turning.

options.label: Smooth, holds its shape

media.alt: Correct eba: smooth, soft, holding shape.
media.brief: Correct eba: smooth, soft, holding shape.

options.guidance: Perfect. Shape and serve.

media.brief: Eba too stiff, cracking.

options.guidance: Add 2 tablespoons of the reserved boiling water and keep turning.
